rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention pattern will guide trimming the solvent window and testing slope or temperature.

Halve the gradient slope without changing the solvent window or temperature to test which crowded pairs respond to slope. This should spread the central cluster and clarify whether temperature-driven selectivity changes will also be needed.
Keep the improved gradient slope and raise temperature to test selectivity in the remaining unresolved cluster. Higher temperature should also bring the last peak closer to the 10-minute target.

Back off temperature by one step to separate the new co-elution at 60 C while retaining most of the time savings. The other pairs at 60 C have sufficient resolution to make this a promising near-target method.

Shift the starting organic fraction upward to perturb the co-eluting pair at 60 C while keeping the slightly shallower gradient favorable for the central cluster. The first peak has ample retention margin, and the last peak should remain within 10 minutes.

Test lower-temperature selectivity to separate the cluster that nearly co-eluted at 40 C. Raising the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 2's gradient slope should offset the longer retention and target a last peak below 10 minutes.

Use a substantially shallower gradient to split the persistent late co-elution at 60 C and improve central-cluster separation. The higher starting organic fraction should offset much of the added retention time while leaving the first compound retained.

Further flatten the gradient to increase separation of the remaining critical pair, which improved in injection 7. Raise the starting organic fraction to limit the last-peak time while monitoring compression of the earlier peaks.

Test the low-temperature end with the same gradient as injection 6 to move the central co-elution apart through selectivity rather than slope. The 8.44-minute last peak at 35 C leaves room for the expected retention increase.
Injection 9 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark and shorten the gradient by one step. This tests whether full resolution can be preserved with a faster last-peak time.

Raise the starting organic fraction and slightly flatten the slope relative to injection 9 to shorten retention without repeating the steepening that lost resolution in injection 10. The first peak remains well away from the unretained region.

Reduce the final organic fraction by one step to flatten the gradient enough to restore the marginal pair in injection 11. This should retain its time advantage over injection 9 while targeting full resolution.

Shift the start upward to shorten retention and narrow the gradient window to protect the slope-sensitive critical pair. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window, making this a candidate for a faster fully resolved method.
Shorten injection 13's gradient by one step, using its resolution margin to reduce the last-peak time. Keep temperature and solvent endpoints fixed to measure the speed–resolution tradeoff directly.

Test a higher starting fraction with a narrower, shallower gradient to offset compression of the critical central pair. This explores whether the fully resolved separation can be moved into a shorter elution window while retaining the maximum CRF.

Keep injection 14 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method and test a substantially steeper gradient for a faster alternative. The slope-sensitive central pair may separate again after an elution-order reversal, though this is exploratory.

Shift both solvent endpoints upward while preserving injection 16's slope to test whether initial-solvent selectivity opens the remaining central pair. This should also shorten retention; injection 14 remains the fully resolved benchmark.

Raise both endpoints another step at the same slope, following the improvement in the critical pair from injections 16 to 17. This tests a faster fully resolved method while checking that the neighboring central pair retains adequate separation.
Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one gradient-time step. Monitor the two pairs near R = 1.6 to determine whether the maximum CRF can be retained at an even shorter last-peak time.

Return to the fully resolved gradient from injection 18 and test a one-step temperature increase as an alternative route to faster elution. This isolates temperature selectivity at the two marginal pairs while retaining injection 18 as the benchmark.

Test beyond the temperature-driven central-pair crossover rather than making another small change toward co-elution. Injection 18 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method; this run explores a potentially faster, reordered separation.

Return to the successful low temperature and test a higher starting fraction with a much shallower gradient to protect central-pair resolution. This explores another route to rapid separation while retaining injection 18 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Trim injection 18's unused high-organic segment while preserving its gradient slope through the observed elution window. This should retain full resolution and the approximately 4.14-minute last peak with a much shorter programmed gradient.

Slightly flatten the successful short gradient to increase the resolution margins of the two limiting pairs. With maximum CRF already secured, this tests a more robust separation at a modest time cost.

Use a slightly shallower gradient than injection 24 to test additional resolution margin while keeping elution well below 10 minutes. Injection 23 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method; this final run targets a less marginal alternative.
